question: I did some college but never finished a degree. I'm trying to stay hopeful and focus on next steps. We just found out our baby is deaf. I am overwhelmed and I do not know where to start. What should we do first?
answer:
Take a breath. What you're feeling right now — overwhelmed, hopeful, scared — is exactly right, and none of this is your fault. Nothing about this diagnosis is a verdict on your family, and nothing you did or didn't do caused it (LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parents FAQ.md).

Here's the good news: almost nothing you decide right now is irreversible except one thing, and it's the thing that matters most — giving your baby accessible language starting today (LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parent Guidance/First 90 Days After Diagnosis.md). You don't need to be fluent, you don't need to have picked a philosophy, and you don't need to decide anything about hearing technology this week. What you do need to do is start signing to your baby now, even with just a handful of signs, alongside whatever auditory support you're pursuing. Every day of visible language in this first year protects a window in brain development that later intervention cannot reopen — the research is clearest on this point of anything in this whole picture (LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parent Guidance/First 90 Days After Diagnosis.md; LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parents FAQ.md).

So, concretely, two things this week:

1. **Start signing today.** Imperfect, beginner signing from you plus some fluent input from others is enough to build language — your baby doesn't need a fluent teacher, just a consistent one (LanguageDeprivationAgent/Core/Bilingual Bimodal Protective Factors.md).
2. **Contact your state's early intervention program** (this is what's called IDEA Part C) and ask specifically for bilingual-bimodal services and a Deaf mentor — a Deaf adult who visits your home, teaches you and your baby visual communication, and connects you to Deaf community (Concepts/IFSP and Part C Early Intervention.md). This is a real, established program — the SKI-HI Deaf Mentor model has been running since 1991, and children in this kind of programming showed considerably stronger vocabulary and language outcomes. You have the right to ask for these specific services, in writing if needed, and to request providers experienced with deaf infants (Concepts/IFSP and Part C Early Intervention.md).

If you're in the DC/Maryland area, the local EHDI program (Newborn Hearing Screening EHDI DC Maryland) offers a free guide and can help route you to Strong Start early intervention and local resources — reach DC EHDI at dcehdi@dc.gov or 1-800-666-2229 (LanguageDeprivationAgent/Local Resources DMV/Newborn Hearing Screening EHDI DC Maryland.md). You might also look into Hands & Voices, a parent-driven support organization with no bias toward any one communication approach, which offers parent-to-parent guidance (Concepts/IFSP and Part C Early Intervention.md).

Whatever grief comes up for the baby you expected — that's normal, it coexists with loving the baby you have, and it tends to loosen over months, especially with a Deaf mentor's support (LanguageDeprivationAg

Concepts/IFSP and Part C Early Intervention.md

question: I'm doing this as a single parent. Honestly part of me still hopes this isn't as big a deal as people are making it sound. We just found out our baby is deaf. I am overwhelmed and I do not know where to start. What should we do first?
answer:
First: take a breath. Nothing about this diagnosis is your fault, and it is not a verdict on your family or your future together — it's simply information you can now act on (LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parents FAQ.md). It's also completely normal to feel like part of you is hoping this isn't as big a deal as it seems — many hearing parents grieve the baby they expected while they build a relationship with the baby they actually have, and both feelings can sit side by side for a while (LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parents FAQ.md).

Here's the one thing that matters most right now: start visible language today. Sign to your baby, even if you know only a handful of signs — you do not need to be fluent, you just need to start the habit, and fluency will build alongside your child's over time (LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parents FAQ.md). Every single day of accessible language in this first year is protecting a window in your baby's brain development that later intervention cannot fully reopen, so starting now, imperfectly, matters far more than waiting until you feel ready (LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parents FAQ.md).

Alongside that, contact your state's early intervention program right away — this is the system set up under a federal law called IDEA Part C, and it exists specifically to get services moving for babies like yours (LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parents FAQ.md). When you reach them, specifically ask for bilingual-bimodal services (meaning support for both sign language and spoken/written language together, not one instead of the other) and a Deaf mentor — a Deaf adult who can come into your home, model fluent sign, and be a living example that Deaf life is not a lesser life, just a different and valuable one (LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parents FAQ.md, LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parent Guidance/Finding Deaf Mentors and Community.md).

As a single parent, know that you don't have to do this alone or perfectly — the early intervention team and a Deaf mentor exist precisely to carry the fluency and expertise while you build your own skills day by day (LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parents FAQ.md). This isn't about closing off any path: starting sign now doesn't lock you out of hearing aids, cochlear implants, or spoken language later — those can all happen alongside sign, not instead of it (LanguageDeprivationAgent/Core/Bilingual Bimodal Protective Factors.md, LanguageDeprivationAgent/Core/Cochlear Implant Pathways and Risk.md). For a fuller week-by-week checklist, look at the guidance for the first ninety days after diagnosis (LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parent Guidance/First 90 Days After Diagnosis.md).
sources: LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parent Guidance/Finding Deaf Mentors and Community.md

question: Honestly part of me still hopes this isn't as big a deal as people are making it sound. I did some college but never finished a degree. We just found out our baby is deaf. I am overwhelmed and I do not know where to start. What should we do first?
answer:
I hear the part of you that's hoping this turns out to be smaller than it looks right now — that's a completely normal place to be, and none of what I'm about to say means your family is facing a tragedy with no path forward. It doesn't. But I do want to be straight with you about what actually helps, because the first year matters more than it seems like it should right now.

The single most important thing to do, starting today, is to make language visible to your baby. That means signing to them, even though you don't know ASL yet and even though you have "some college" and no background in linguistics — none of that disqualifies you. Most hearing parents learn ASL alongside their child rather than before, and the goal right now isn't fluency, it's building a daily habit (LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parents FAQ.md). Fluent signers — a Deaf mentor, a bilingual-bimodal early interventionist — fill in the quality gap while your own skills grow.

At the same time, contact your state's early intervention program and specifically ask for bilingual-bimodal services and a Deaf mentor (LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parents FAQ.md). This is the practical next step, and it's the same one laid out for the first ninety days after diagnosis, which includes weekly rhythms like a parent-infant signing class, regular contact with a Deaf mentor or Deaf family, and audiology and early-intervention appointments (LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parent Guidance/First 90 Days After Diagnosis.md).

Why the urgency, when part of you wants to wait and see? Every day of visible, accessible language exposure in your baby's first year protects something called the critical period — a window in early brain development that no later intervention can fully reopen (LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parents FAQ.md). This isn't a reason to panic; it's a reason to act now rather than later, and starting sign doesn't shut any doors — it doesn't commit your family to any single identity or rule out hearing technology later. Sign and spoken-language paths can run together (LanguageDeprivationAgent/Choosing a Communication Approach.md).

And please hear this clearly: none of this is your fault, and the diagnosis is not a verdict on your family (LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parents FAQ.md). It's also normal to be grieving the baby you expected while you fall in love with the baby you have — both feelings can sit side by side, and a Deaf mentor often helps that grief settle into something more like recognition that Deaf adulthood is a different, valuable life, not a failure state (LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parents FAQ.md).

For your very next step: call your state's early intervention program today and ask directly for bilingual-bimodal services and a Deaf mentor referral, and start signing to your baby tonight, however imperfectly.
sources: LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parent Guidance/Where to Find Help National Organizations.md
LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parent Guidance/Finding Deaf Mentors and Community.md

question: I keep wondering if this is somehow my fault. We want to raise our child fully immersed in ASL and Deaf culture. We just found out our baby is deaf. I am overwhelmed and I do not know where to start. What should we do first?
answer:
First — this is not your fault. Nothing about your baby's diagnosis is a verdict on your family, and there's nothing you did or failed to do that caused this. You're overwhelmed because you love your baby and want to get this right, and wanting to raise your child fully immersed in ASL and Deaf culture is a beautiful, well-founded goal (LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parents FAQ.md).

Here's what to do first, today: start signing to your baby right now, even though you're not fluent yet. You don't need to know much ASL — the habit of visible language matters far more than your skill level at this point. A parent who barely remembers high school Spanish is on the normal path here, not a failing one (LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parents FAQ.md). Every single day of accessible language exposure in this first year protects a critical window for language development that no later intervention can fully reopen — so the urgency is real, but it's motivating, not a countdown to panic (LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parents FAQ.md).

At the same time, contact your state's early intervention program — this is the system set up under a federal law called IDEA Part C, which provides services for infants and toddlers with disabilities. When you contact them, specifically ask for bilingual-bimodal services (an approach that gives your child both a sign language and a spoken/written language in parallel, with neither one blocking the other) and a Deaf mentor — a fluent Deaf adult who can model real, natural signing for your family while you're still learning (LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parents FAQ.md; LanguageDeprivationAgent/Core/Bilingual Bimodal Protective Factors.md).

Since your goal is full ASL and Deaf culture immersion, know that this is a well-worn, supported path: many hearing parents build exactly this life for their deaf child, and organizations, Deaf mentor programs, college ASL classes, and Deaf community events all exist to help you get there (Sources/Lieberman Mitchiner Pontecorvo 2022 - Hearing Parents Learning ASL.md). Bring in Deaf adults and older Deaf children as language models as early as possible, since your own early signing — while essential to start now — can't be your child's only fluent input (LanguageDeprivationAgent/Core/Bilingual Bimodal Protective Factors.md).

So, concretely: sign to your baby today, at whatever level you have. Call early intervention this week and request bilingual-bimodal services and a Deaf mentor. Look for Deaf community events and mentor programs to connect with fluent signers. You are not behind, and this is not a tragedy — it's a beginning, and you're already asking the right questions.
sources: Sources/Lieberman Mitchiner Pontecorvo 2022 - Hearing Parents Learning ASL.md
Sources/Language Deprivation/Humphries et al 2016 - Language Choices for Deaf Infants.md

question: I'm frustrated and honestly a little angry at how confusing this all is. We're a middle-income family with a decent but not unlimited budget. We just found out our baby is deaf. I am overwhelmed and I do not know where to start. What should we do first?
answer:
Your anger and overwhelm make complete sense — you just got life-changing news and everyone seems to be giving conflicting advice. Take a breath: none of this is your fault, and nothing about this diagnosis is a verdict on your family or your baby's future (LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parents FAQ.md).

Here's the one thing that matters most right now, and it's genuinely doable on any budget: start giving your baby visible language today. You don't need to be fluent in ASL (American Sign Language) to begin — just start signing to your baby now, alongside whatever hearing technology or auditory work you decide to pursue later (LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parent Guidance/First 90 Days After Diagnosis.md). Every single day of accessible language exposure in this first year is protecting something called the critical period — a developmental window that, once closed, no later intervention can reopen (LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parents FAQ.md; LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parent Guidance/First 90 Days After Diagnosis.md).

At the same time, contact your state's early intervention program — this is the free, publicly funded system set up under IDEA Part C specifically for infants and toddlers with developmental needs, including deaf and hard-of-hearing babies (LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parents FAQ.md; Concepts/EHDI Early Hearing Detection and Intervention.md). When you call, specifically request bilingual-bimodal services (meaning support for both signed and spoken language together, not one instead of the other) and ask for a Deaf mentor — a Deaf adult who can model language and connect your family to the Deaf community (LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parents FAQ.md; Concepts/EHDI Early Hearing Detection and Intervention.md). Put your request in writing and ask them directly how they will track your child's language milestones in both ASL and English — enrollment alone isn't enough (Concepts/EHDI Early Hearing Detection and Intervention.md).

You do not have to decide about cochlear implants this week, and you don't have to pick a single "philosophy" right now (LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parent Guidance/First 90 Days After Diagnosis.md). Hearing aids or future implants improve auditory access, but they don't replace language — signing keeps working even when devices are off, in the bath, at night, or if the equipment fails, so there's no need to wait and see (LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parent Guidance/Months 3 to 12 Early Exposure.md). Many parents also grieve the hearing child they expected while falling in love with the deaf child they have — that's normal, both feelings can coexist, and a Deaf mentor often helps that grief settle into something more like recognition of a different, valuable life ahead (LanguageDeprivationAgent/Parents FAQ.md).
